newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Red Cross warns of imminent catastrophe in N.Korea.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross warns of imminent catastrophe in N.Korea.

text.p: Red Cross officials on Wednesday warned of imminent famine in North Korea, saying kitchens were bare except for grass and tree bark, children were weak and cattle were being slaughtered to save feed grain.

Yasuo Tanaka, an officer of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies who visited the impoverished nation last week, confirmed reports that food stocks had almost completely dried up.
"In some kitchens, there was no rice, no food at all. I asked them what they ate and they showed me natural grasses," he told a news conference.
In other kitchens he saw tree bark, roots and dried vegetables.
"Children looked weak and tired," he said.
"A boy I met who said he was 10 years old looked like a seven-year-old. A girl who said she was five years old looked like she was three years old: she was very light."
"Without urgent international aid programmes, a large number of North Koreans will face starvation," said Johan Schaar, chief of the Asia-Pacific region of the Geneva-based Red Cross.
"Food stocks in North Korea can run out any time now."
Schaar said some 600,000 livestock recently had been slaughtered to divert feed grain for human consumption.

The Red Cross assessment of looming catastrophe matches a report on Tuesday by the U.N. World Food Programme, which said it planned to double its $41 million aid appeal for North Korea citing fears of starvation "on a massive scale".
Adding to a sense of crisis, Seoul's defence ministry said North Korea had just completed a military training exercise on a broader scale than usual.
North Korean citizens conducted air-raid and evacuation drills while camouflaged troops trained in tunnel warfare, the ministry said in a statement.
"Such exercises were held in 1995 and 1996 in limited areas. This year they were conducted nationwide, which is unusual. Our military has thus strengthened its surveillance," it said.
Tanaka said North Korean officials put the 1996 harvest at 2.5 million tonnes, leaving a shortfall of 2.32 million tonnes. Grain stocks at the end of December totalled 240,000 tonnes.
Schaar and Tanaka are in South Korea to supervise an aid shipment of food and vegetable seed worth more than $1 million that is due to leave on Thursday or Friday.
It would be the largest food delivery by South Korean religious and civic groups since such shipments began in 1995.

Shaar welcomed Seoul's decision on Monday to lift a ban on private organisations providing rice to Pyongyang. Previously, private groups could only ship non-rice food aid because of fears that rice could be diverted to the military.
"I think this is a very symbolic sign of more support coming," Shaar said.
He urged governments not to use food aid to exert political pressure on North Korea.
"You should not let the children of North Korea be victims of any kind of political differences between these governments and North Korea," he added, without naming any countries.

Seoul's decision on rice aid was widely interpreted as an effort to coax Pyongyang into four-nation talks with the United States and China aimed at securing a lasting peace to replace an armistice that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
North Korea is insisting on substantial food aid before joining the talks, but Seoul and Washington insist aid can only be discussed during the peace talks.
